name: HTML
description: Documents, landmarks, forms and the semantics that hold a page together.

lessons.title: The shape of a page
lessons.summary: Every website is one document with a head and a body. Build your first one.
objectives: Write a valid HTML document from scratch
Explain what the head and body are for
Nest elements correctly

sections.body: Every page you have ever visited is a text file that a browser reads top to bottom. HTML gives that text structure: this is a heading, this is a paragraph, this is a link. You are not styling anything yet. You are describing what things **are**.
A complete document has four parts that never change:

sections.code:
Field notes from the coast

Three days of wind, salt and very average coffee.
sections.caption: The smallest page worth writing

items: `<!DOCTYPE html>` tells the browser to use modern standards mode. Leave it out and you get 1999 behaviour.
`<head>` holds information **about** the page: the title, character set, descriptions, styles.
`<body>` holds everything a visitor can actually see.
`lang="en"` on `<html>` tells screen readers which language to pronounce.

sections.title: Indentation is for humans
sections.body: The browser does not care about whitespace between tags, but the next person reading your file does. Two spaces per level, one element per line, and your future self will thank you.
One rule matters more than the rest: elements **nest** or sit side by side, they never overlap. If you open a tag inside a paragraph, close it before you close the paragraph.

drills.prompt: Which element declares the language of the whole document?
drills.explain: The `lang` attribute on `<html>` tells screen readers and search engines which language the page is written in. The charset meta describes encoding, not language.
hints: The attribute lives on the outermost element.

drills.prompt: Put the skeleton of a page in the order the browser reads it.
drills.explain: Doctype first, then the root element, then head and body in that order. The doctype is what puts the browser in standards mode.
hints: The head closes before the body opens.

drills.prompt: One line stops this page from being valid. Which one?
drills.explain: `<title>` is never self-closing. Without `</title>` everything after it is parsed as title text.
hints: Look for an element that opens and never closes.

quiz.prompt: Where does the page title belong?
quiz.explain: The title lives in <head>. It shows in the browser tab and in search results, never in the page body.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about nesting is true?
options: Elements can overlap as long as they are closed eventually
Elements must be fully nested or be siblings
Only block elements need closing tags
The browser fixes any nesting you write
quiz.explain: Elements are either fully inside another element or siblings next to it. Overlapping tags produce unpredictable trees.

lessons.title: Text that reads well
lessons.summary: Headings, paragraphs, lists and emphasis — the typography of HTML.
objectives: Use a heading hierarchy instead of bold text
Mark up lists with ul and ol
Choose strong and em for meaning, not decoration

sections.body: Sighted users skim. Screen reader users jump between headings. Both behaviours depend on you choosing the right element rather than making text *look* big.

sections.code:
Brew guide

Water

Start with soft water. Hard water mutes the acidity.

Ratio

Use 60 grams per litre. Adjust after tasting.

  • Weigh the beans
  • Rinse the filter
  • Pour slowly

items: `<h1>` once per page. `<h2>` for sections, `<h3>` for subsections. Never skip a level for looks.

`

` is for prose. If you need a line break inside a paragraph, `
` exists, but a new paragraph is usually correct.
`<ul>` is unordered (order does not matter), `<ol>` is ordered (steps, rankings).
`<strong>` marks importance, `<em>` marks emphasis. A screen reader can change its voice for both.

sections.title: Do not use headings to style text
sections.body: If a line should look bold but is not a section title, use `<strong>`. If it should look big, that is CSS. Heading levels describe document structure, and assistive tech relies on them.
Write the content first, then check: could someone navigate this page using only its headings? If the answer is no, the structure is wrong, not the styling.

drills.prompt: Mark the opening and closing tag of a level-two heading.
drills.explain: Heading elements are numbered `h1` to `h6`. An `h1` names the page; `h2` starts a section inside it.
hints: The closing tag matches the opening one exactly.

drills.prompt: Which element should wrap a list where order matters?
drills.explain: `<ol>` is an ordered list: the browser numbers the items for you. Use `<ul>` when the sequence carries no meaning.

drills.prompt: Which element gives a paragraph of text?
drills.explain:
`

` is the paragraph element. Browsers add spacing around it by default, which is why it reads as a block of prose.
hints: It is the shortest block element you know.

checks.label: An <h2> heading exists
The heading reads “Field notes”
There are at least two paragraphs
One paragraph uses <strong> for emphasis
The list has at least three items

hints: Each list item is its own `<li>` inside a single `<ul>`.
`<strong>` goes *inside* the paragraph, around the words you want to stress.

quiz.prompt: You need a step-by-step recipe. Which list is correct?
quiz.explain: <ol> is the ordered list. Order matters for steps, and screen readers announce the item numbers.

options: <b> is deprecated and renders as normal text
<strong> carries meaning that assistive technology can announce
It is the only tag that accepts a class
quiz.explain: <strong> means “important”; <b> only means “bold”. Same pixels, different semantics.

lessons.title: Links and images
lessons.summary: The two elements that turn a document into the web.
objectives: Write relative and absolute links
Explain what the alt attribute is for
Group navigation links in a nav element

sections.body: A page with no links is a dead end. `` and `` are the two elements that make a document part of the web, and both have one attribute you must never skip.

sections.code: Lessons MDN

items: `href` accepts a full URL, a path like `/learn`, a fragment like `#pricing`, or `mailto:you@site.com`.
Link text should make sense out of context. “Read the CSS guide” beats “click here”.
`alt` describes the image for people who cannot see it. Empty `alt=""` is correct for purely decorative images.
`target="_blank"` opens a new tab. Add `rel="noreferrer"` so the new page cannot access your tab.

sections.title: Alt text is a caption, not a filename
sections.body: Write what the image shows and why it matters here: “Fog rolling over a grey beach at dawn”, not “coast.jpg” and not “image”.
Paths are relative to the document that contains them. `coast.jpg` looks next to the current file, `/coast.jpg` starts from the site root, `../coast.jpg` climbs one folder.

drills.prompt: Give the image a text alternative.
drills.explain: `alt` is what a screen reader announces and what shows if the image fails. Decorative images take `alt=""`.

drills.prompt: Which line links to a page that will not load?
drills.explain: `hraf` is a typo. The attribute is `href`, so the browser treats the second link as having no destination.
hints: Read the attribute names character by character.

drills.prompt: Which attribute holds a link's destination?
drills.explain: `href` is the hypertext reference: the URL the link points at. `src` is for embedded resources like images and scripts.

checks.label: A <nav> wraps the links
There are two links inside the nav
One link points to an external site

hints: `href="#lessons"` links to an element with `id="lessons"` on the same page.

quiz.prompt: Which href is relative to the site root?
quiz.explain: A leading slash always resolves from the domain root, no matter which page you are on.

quiz.prompt: When is alt="" the right choice?
options: Never, every image needs a description
When the image is decorative and adds no information
When the image is a photo
When the filename already describes it
quiz.explain: An empty alt tells assistive tech to skip the image entirely, which is correct for decoration.

lessons.title: Semantic structure
lessons.summary: Landmarks that make a page navigable for humans, screen readers and search engines.
objectives: Replace generic divs with landmark elements
Understand header, main, section, article, footer
Keep exactly one main per page

sections.body: A page built from `<div>`s works until someone tries to navigate it. Screen readers offer a list of landmarks; search engines use the same structure to understand which part is the actual content.

sections.code:
Zuno
Learn

Field notes

Tide tables

The tide turned an hour early.

© 2026 Zuno

items: `<header>` and `<footer>` can appear on the page or inside an article. They describe their nearest section.
`<main>` holds the content unique to this page. Exactly one per document.
`<article>` is a self-contained unit: a post, a card, a comment. It should make sense on its own.
`<section>` groups related content and usually starts with a heading.
`<nav>` is for major link groups. Not every group of links needs one.

sections.title: Landmarks replace ARIA
sections.body: A `<nav>` already exposes `role="navigation"`. Writing both is noise. Native elements first, ARIA only when nothing native fits.
Rule of thumb: if you are about to write `<div class="header">`, check whether `<header>` does the job. The class name is a strong hint that you already knew the meaning.

drills.prompt: Which element wraps the main navigation of a site?
drills.explain: `<nav>` marks a block of navigation links. Screen readers can jump straight to it, and so can crawlers.
hints: `<menu>` is for command lists, not site links.

drills.prompt: Order the landmarks of a typical page.
drills.explain: Header, main, footer is the reading order. Landmarks describe regions, never appearance.

drills.prompt: Which element holds the unique content of the page, used once per document?
drills.explain: `<main>` is the single region holding the page's primary content. It also gives assistive tech a skip-to-content target.

The header contains a <nav> with a link

quiz.prompt: How many <main> elements should a page have?
quiz.explain: <main> marks the unique content of the document. More than one breaks the landmark map.

quiz.prompt: A blog card that could be syndicated on its own should be a…
quiz.explain: <article> means self-contained and independently distributable — exactly what a syndicated card is.

lessons.title: Forms people can finish
lessons.summary: Labels, input types and validation that work before JavaScript exists.
objectives: Connect every input to a label
Pick input types that unlock the right keyboard
Use native validation before writing any JavaScript

sections.body: Forms are where a website asks for something. Most form pain is self-inflicted: missing labels, `type="text"` for an email, a submit handler that fights the browser.

sections.code: We send one short lesson each weekday.

items: `label for="email"` must match the input's `id`. Clicking the label then focuses the field.
`type="email"` gives you a validation rule and the @ keyboard on phones, for free.
`required`, `minlength`, `pattern` and `min` are enforced by the browser before submission.
`autocomplete` lets password managers and browsers fill the field correctly.
Every input needs a `name` or it will never reach the server.

sections.title: Placeholder is not a label
sections.body: Placeholders vanish the moment someone types, have poor contrast, and are skipped by some screen readers. Use a real `<label>`; the placeholder is a hint at most.
Group related fields with `<fieldset>` and `<legend>` — especially radio buttons, where the legend answers “what am I choosing between?”.

drills.prompt: Ask the browser for an email field and a required name field.
drills.explain: `type="email"` gives you keyboard and validation for free. `required` blocks submission while the field is empty, without any JavaScript.
hints: The first one names the kind of control.
The second is a boolean attribute.

options: It ties the label to the control so clicking it focuses the field
drills.explain: `for` matches the input's `id`, so the two are announced together and clicking the label focuses the field.
hints: Think about what a screen reader says.
It is about association, not looks.

exercise.brief: Build a sign-up `<form>` with: a labeled email input (`type="email"`, `required`), a labeled password input (`type="password"`, `minlength="8"`), and a submit button. Every input needs an `id`, a `name` and a `<label for>`.
exercise.starter: Create your account
exercise.solution: Create your account

checks.label: A <form> wraps the fields
The email input is type=email and required
Both inputs have a label with a matching for
The password field masks input and demands 8+ characters
A submit button exists

hints: Each `label` needs `for="id-of-input"` — the id and for values must match exactly.
`minlength` is an attribute, not a CSS property: `minlength="8"`.

quiz.prompt: Why does an input need a name attribute?
options: So its value is included when the form is submitted
So the label can point at it
It is optional and purely decorative
quiz.explain: The name becomes the key in the submitted form data. No name, no value sent.

quiz.prompt: Which is the best label for a group of radio buttons?
options: A placeholder on the first radio
quiz.explain: <fieldset> + <legend> groups the choices and names the question natively.

lessons.title: Tables and data
lessons.summary: Real tabular data, with headers that announce themselves.
objectives: Separate structure into thead, tbody and tfoot
Use scope to bind headers to cells
Never use a table for layout

sections.body: Tables are for data that has rows and columns. That is a narrow use case, and when it applies, nothing else comes close.

items: `<caption>` describes the table. It is the first thing a screen reader announces.
`<thead>`, `<tbody>` and `<tfoot>` group rows so browsers and assistive tech can treat them differently.
`scope="col"` on a header means “this header labels the column below me”; `scope="row"` labels the row beside it.
Use `<th>` for headers, `<td>` for data. The distinction is announced, not just bolded.

sections.title: Tables are not layouts
sections.body: Using a table to place a sidebar was normal in 2004. Today it breaks responsiveness and screen readers announce a data grid that does not exist. Use CSS grid.
If a table needs horizontal scrolling on small screens, wrap it in a container with `overflow-x: auto` rather than shrinking the text.

drills.explain: Head, body, rows, cells. `scope="col"` tells assistive tech that the header describes the column below it.

drills.prompt: Which element marks a header cell in a table?
drills.explain: `<th>` is a header cell; `<td>` is a data cell. Headers are read out before each cell value.

The table has a <caption>

quiz.prompt: What does scope="row" tell assistive technology?
options: This cell spans the whole row
This header labels the cells to its right
This row is the header row
quiz.explain: A row header names the data cells beside it — useful for tables with a label column.

quiz.prompt: You need two columns of content in a layout. What should you use?
quiz.explain: Layout belongs to CSS. Tables are for data only.

lessons.title: Media, metadata and accessible widgets
lessons.summary: Figures, disclosure widgets and the tags search engines and screen readers read first.
objectives: Pair media with captions using figure and figcaption
Use details and summary instead of a JS accordion
Give icon-only buttons an accessible name

sections.body: The last HTML lesson is about the details that separate a page that works from a page that is pleasant to use with a keyboard, a screen reader, or a search engine.

sections.code:
What is included in Pro?

All lessons, the playground and offline progress.

items: `<figure>` groups media with its caption. `<figcaption>` must be the first or last child.
`<details>`/`<summary>` is a native disclosure widget: keyboard support, open/close state and animation hooks, zero JavaScript.
An icon-only button needs a name. `aria-label` provides it; `aria-hidden="true"` hides the decorative SVG.
`<meta name="description">` is the snippet search engines usually show. Keep it under ~155 characters.

sections.title: Test with the Tab key
sections.body: Everything interactive must be reachable with Tab and operable with Enter or Space. If you cannot do it without a mouse, neither can a lot of your visitors.
Prefer the native element every time. `<details>` beats a hand-rolled accordion, `<dialog>` beats a modal div, `<button>` beats a clickable div. Less code, more behaviour.

drills.prompt: A decorative background image should have which alt text?
drills.explain: An empty `alt` marks the image as decorative, so screen readers skip it. Leaving the attribute out makes some readers announce the file name instead.
hints: Decorative means it adds no information.

drills.prompt: Load a video with controls and captions.
drills.code:
<video {{0}} muted playsinline>
  <source src="intro.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  <{{1}} src="intro.vtt" kind="captions" srclang="en">
</video>
drills.explain: `controls` gives the play button back to the user. `<track kind="captions">` supplies the caption file.
hints: The user needs a play button.

checks.label: The meta description is at least 40 characters

quiz.prompt: Why prefer <details> over a JavaScript accordion?
options: Keyboard support, state and semantics come free and correct
quiz.explain: Native disclosure handles focus, Enter/Space, and exposes expanded state. You inherit all of it.

quiz.prompt: An icon-only button needs which attribute to be announced correctly?
quiz.explain: aria-label supplies the accessible name. title is a tooltip and is not reliably announced.
